entries.sentence: A sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis.
entries.note: NHS and WHO describe chlamydia as a bacterial sexually transmitted infection; WHO names Chlamydia trachomatis.

entries.sentence: Chlamydia is a bacterial infection that is usually spread through sex.
entries.note: NHS: bacterial infection usually passed on through sex.

entries.sentence: Many people have no symptoms and do not know they have it.
entries.note: NHS: most people notice no symptoms; WHO: many have none.

entries.sentence: When symptoms do occur they can include unusual discharge, pain when passing urine, and pelvic or testicular pain.
entries.note: Search summary of NHS: discharge, pain on urinating, pelvic or testicular pain; MedlinePlus lists burning on urination and testicular pain.

entries.sentence: It is curable with antibiotics, but untreated infection can cause problems such as pelvic inflammatory disease and can affect fertility.
entries.note: NHS: curable with antibiotics; complications page: PID, infertility risk.

entries.sentence: Testing uses a urine sample or a swab.
entries.note: NHS summary: urine sample or swab.

entries.sentence: Infection with the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis.
entries.note: WHO fact sheet names the bacterium.

entries.sentence: It is usually spread through vaginal, oral or anal sex, or contact with infected genital fluids such as semen or vaginal fluid.
entries.note: WHO: vaginal, oral and anal sex; NHS: infected genital fluids (semen, vaginal fluid).

entries.sentence: Sharing sex toys that are not washed or covered with a new condom each time they are used can also pass it on.
entries.note: NHS summary: sharing sex toys not washed or covered with a new condom.

entries.sentence: An untreated infection can pass from a pregnant person to the baby during birth.
entries.note: NHS complications and CDC: can pass infection to the baby.

entries.sentence: It is not spread by casual contact such as kissing, hugging or sharing towels or toilet seats.
Sex without a condom.
entries.note: NHS: often passed on through unprotected sex.

entries.sentence: A new sexual partner.
entries.note: CDC lists a new partner as increased risk.

entries.sentence: More than one sexual partner.
entries.note: CDC lists more than one partner as increased risk.

entries.sentence: A sexual partner who has a sexually transmitted infection.
entries.note: CDC lists a partner with an STI as increased risk.

entries.sentence: Being a sexually active woman under 25, the group the English screening programme prioritises.
entries.note: NCSP overview: opportunistic screening focuses on sexually active women under 25.

entries.sentence: Unusual vaginal discharge or discharge from the penis.
entries.note: NHS: unusual discharge; CDC: vaginal discharge; MedlinePlus: discharge from penis.

entries.sentence: Bleeding after sex or between periods.
entries.note: NHS and CDC list bleeding after sex and between periods.

entries.sentence: Pain or swelling in the testicles.
entries.note: NHS: pain and swelling in testicles; MedlinePlus: testicular tenderness or pain.

entries.sentence: Rectal pain or discharge.
entries.note: CDC (women) and MedlinePlus (men) list rectal pain or discharge.

entries.sentence: Pelvic inflammatory disease in women, when the infection spreads to the womb, ovaries or fallopian tubes.
Difficulty getting pregnant or infertility, long-lasting pelvic pain and a higher risk of ectopic pregnancy after pelvic inflammatory disease.
entries.note: NHS complications: PID can lead to these; WHO lists PID, pelvic pain, infertility and ectopic pregnancy.

entries.sentence: Pain and swelling of the epididymis in men, which the NHS describes as very rare.
Premature labour and low birthweight when infection is untreated in pregnancy.
entries.note: NHS and WHO: linked to early birth and low birthweight.

entries.sentence: Eye infection or pneumonia in a newborn who caught the infection during birth.
entries.note: NHS: baby may develop conjunctivitis and pneumonia.

entries.sentence: Chlamydia is diagnosed by testing a urine sample or a swab.
entries.note: NHS and WHO: urine samples or swabs.

entries.sentence: The test most often used is a nucleic acid amplification test, known as a NAAT, which WHO describes as the gold standard.
Some services offer online test kits.
entries.note: NHS search summary: some services offer online kits.

entries.sentence: A sexual health service notes that a very recent infection may not show up on a test straight away.
entries.note: A local NHS sexual health service page (Wirral) says it may take time to show on a test; blended summary.

entries.sentence: In England the national screening programme recommends that sexually active women under 25 are tested each year and after each new partner.
Chlamydia is curable with antibiotics.
The standard antibiotic options are doxycycline and azithromycin tablets.
entries.note: NHS summary and WHO name both.

entries.sentence: The 2026 BASHH guideline makes doxycycline the first-line treatment, with azithromycin used only where another infection, Mycoplasma genitalium, has been excluded.
Partners are also tested and treated.
entries.note: NHS and WHO: partners should be notified, tested and treated.

entries.sentence: Sexual activity is paused until treatment and any tests are complete.
People diagnosed are offered a repeat test some months after treatment to check for reinfection.
entries.note: NHS: under-25s offered another test 3 to 6 months after; NCSP retesting.

entries.sentence: Correct and consistent use of condoms during sex is the most effective way to prevent chlamydia.
The NHS also describes condoms or dental dams for oral sex, and washing sex toys or covering them with a new condom each time.
There is no vaccine against chlamydia.
entries.note: WHO: no vaccines for chlamydial infection.

entries.sentence: The NHS advises testing once a year or when there is a new sexual partner.
entries.note: NHS summary of when to test.

entries.sentence: A sexual health service can arrange testing for people with or without symptoms, for a new sexual partner, or after a partner is diagnosed; the NHS advises testing once a year or with a new partner.
entries.note: NHS: test yearly or with new partner; NCSP: sexual health services provide tests; CDC: test if no symptoms but increased risk.

entries.sentence: Severe pelvic or testicular pain, or feeling very unwell, needs urgent help from NHS 111 or the GP the same day, and a call to 999 in an emergency.
entries.note: Routing advice, not drawn from retrieved text.

entries.sentence: Most people with chlamydia do not notice any symptoms and do not know they have it.
When symptoms do occur, they may take weeks to appear after sex with someone who has chlamydia.
entries.note: NHS, CDC and WHO: symptoms may not appear until weeks after exposure.

entries.sentence: Because symptoms are often absent, the infection can go unnoticed until a test is done.
entries.note: Follows from NHS: most do not know; CDC: often causes no symptoms.

entries.sentence: In women, symptoms can include unusual vaginal discharge, pain when passing urine, pain in the tummy or pelvis, bleeding after sex and bleeding between periods.
Painful sex and rectal pain or discharge have also been listed by the CDC.
entries.note: CDC: painful sex, rectal pain or discharge.

entries.sentence: The CDC adds that chlamydia can damage the reproductive system of a woman even when it causes no symptoms.
In men, symptoms can include discharge from the penis, burning when passing urine, and pain or swelling in the testicles.
Infection of the rectum can also cause symptoms in both women and men.
entries.note: CDC: rectal infections can cause symptoms; MedlinePlus lists rectal discharge in men.

entries.sentence: Chlamydia is caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis.
It is usually spread through vaginal, oral or anal sex, or through contact with infected genital fluids such as semen or vaginal fluid.
The NHS describes sex without a condom as a common route of infection.
entries.note: NHS: often passed on through unprotected sex.

entries.sentence: It can also be passed on by sharing sex toys that are not washed or covered with a new condom each time they are used.
Casual contact such as kissing, hugging or sharing towels or toilet seats does not spread it.
The CDC lists a new sexual partner, more than one partner and a partner with a sexually transmitted infection as situations of increased risk.
An untreated infection can also pass from a pregnant person to the baby during birth.
Chlamydia is diagnosed by testing a urine sample or a swab.
The test most often used is a nucleic acid amplification test, known as a NAAT, which WHO describes as the gold standard.
Some services offer online test kits.
A sexual health service notes that a very recent infection may not show up on a test straight away.
entries.note: Local NHS sexual health page; blended summary.

entries.sentence: In England the National Chlamydia Screening Programme focuses on sexually active women under 25, who are recommended to test each year and after each new partner.
Young men can still get tests at sexual health services, and are contacted and tested through partner notification.
More generally, the NHS advises testing once a year or when there is a new sexual partner.
Anyone diagnosed is offered a discussion about partner notification, so that recent partners can be tested and treated.
entries.note: NCSP and BASHH: partner notification discussed at diagnosis.

entries.sentence: Chlamydia is curable with antibiotics.
The standard antibiotic options are doxycycline and azithromycin tablets.
The 2026 BASHH guideline makes doxycycline the first-line treatment, with azithromycin used only where another infection, Mycoplasma genitalium, has been excluded.
Partners are also tested and treated.
Sexual activity is paused until treatment and any tests are complete.
WHO advises waiting after finishing the medicine before having sex, or using condoms correctly.
Older BASHH guidance says current partners should be treated whatever their own test result.
entries.note: BASHH search summary: all current partners treated irrespective of test results (older BASHH guidance).

entries.sentence: The same guidance advised that the person and treated partners avoid sex, including oral sex and sex with condoms, for a time after treatment.
entries.note: BASHH patient guidance summary: no sex including oral sex and with condoms for a week; exact wording to confirm.

entries.sentence: People diagnosed are offered another test some months after treatment, to look for reinfection.
entries.note: NHS: under-25s offered another test 3 to 6 months later; NCSP overview on retesting.

entries.sentence: One Scottish guideline says a routine test of cure is not required.
entries.note: Scottish guideline snippet: Test of cure: not routinely required.

entries.sentence: Untreated chlamydia can cause serious problems, but WHO says long-term problems are unlikely if it is treated early.
In women the infection can spread to the womb, ovaries or fallopian tubes and cause pelvic inflammatory disease.
This can lead to difficulty getting pregnant, long-lasting pelvic pain and a higher risk of ectopic pregnancy.
Pelvic inflammatory disease is usually treated with a course of antibiotics.
In men, the infection can spread to the testicles and epididymis, causing pain and swelling, though the NHS describes this as very rare.
The NHS says untreated infection might affect fertility in men, while the CDC says men rarely have health problems from chlamydia.
In pregnancy, untreated chlamydia may increase the risk of premature labour and low birthweight, and the baby may develop an eye infection or pneumonia after birth.
WHO says correct and consistent use of condoms during sex is the most effective way to prevent chlamydia.
The NHS also describes condoms or dental dams for oral sex, and washing sex toys or covering them with a new condom each time.
There is no vaccine against chlamydia.
Because many infections cause no symptoms, the NHS advises testing once a year or with a new sexual partner.
A sexual health service can arrange testing, whether or not there are symptoms.
entries.note: NCSP: sexual health services provide tests; CDC: testing is advised even without symptoms when risk is increased.

entries.sentence: The English programme also aims to reduce harm from untreated infection through faster results and treatment, partner notification and retesting.
entries.note: NCSP overview: screening focus on reducing time to test results and treatment, strengthening partner notification and retesting.

entries.sentence: WHO has a global strategy that aims to reduce new chlamydia cases by 2030.
entries.note: WHO fact sheet: strategy aims for reduction in new cases by 2030.

entries.sentence: Tests for other sexually transmitted infections are often recommended at the same time.
entries.note: Search summary attributed this to WHO; pages blended, check at second pass.
